planting.note: Root stem cuttings directly in consistently wet, saline to brackish sandy or muddy soil in full sun; saltwort is a true salt marsh specialist and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone — it needs tidal, brackish, or salted conditions to perform.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings directly into consistently wet, saline to brackish sand or mud in full sun along tidal flats, salt marsh edges, or artificially salted raised beds; saltwort is one of the few true halophytes grown for food, an edible succulent similar in use to samphire or sea beans. Jointed, cylindrical, fleshy stems form a low, spreading, olive-green mat, and the crisp, salty-tangy young stem tips are harvested and eaten fresh in salads, pickled, or lightly sautéed. It naturally colonizes the upper edges of salt marshes and mangrove fringe, tolerating regular tidal inundation and salinity that would kill nearly any other vegetable crop, but it needs that salinity to compete against weeds and grow vigorously. Harvest tips regularly to encourage bushy branching, and expect the planting to spread steadily by rooting stems across suitable wet, saline ground.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end an inch into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in late spring; erect pricklypear tolerates salt spray and sandy coastal soil better than most garden plants.

directions: Plant a callused pad in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; erect pricklypear is a taller, more upright-growing native pricklypear of Gulf and Atlantic coastal dunes and sandy scrub, forming a shrubby, multi-jointed clump 2 to 4 feet high. Bright yellow, sometimes red-throated flowers open in late spring and early summer, followed by reddish-purple, edible fruit (tunas) enjoyed fresh, juiced, or made into jelly once the glochids are carefully removed or burned off. It handles salt spray, sandy soil, and coastal wind better than almost any other flowering succulent, making it valuable for beachfront xeriscape and dune stabilization plantings. Handle pads and fruit with heavy gloves and tongs to avoid the fine, easily embedded glochids, and site it away from foot traffic areas.

planting.note: Direct sow into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun near the coast; sea rocket is adapted to shifting dune sand, salt spray, and periodic sand burial, so avoid rich garden soil and heavy mulch, which encourage rot.

directions: Direct sow into loose, well-drained beach or dune-type sand in full sun; American sea rocket is a fleshy-leaved, mustard-family annual that colonizes the upper beach and foredune along both Atlantic and Pacific coasts, tolerating salt spray, sand burial, and drought that would kill nearly any conventional vegetable. The succulent, deeply lobed leaves and young seed pods have a sharp, peppery, radish-like bite and are eaten fresh in salads or as a pungent garnish, much like a wild, salt-tolerant arugula. Small four-petaled pale lavender to white flowers appear over a long season, followed by distinctive two-segmented, corky seed pods that float and disperse on tides and currents. It self-sows readily in loose sand and is best grown in a sandy raised bed or true beach-adjacent garden rather than ordinary rich soil, where it becomes leggy and short-lived.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society (Native Plant Trust)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun on the upper beach and foredune; this is the Florida and Caribbean native beach naupaka and should not be confused with the widely sold, invasive Pacific beach naupaka (Scaevola taccada).

directions: Plant in loose, sandy, salt-influenced soil in full sun on the foredune or upper beach; native beach naupaka is a low, rounded, salt- and wind-tolerant shrub with thick, glossy, fleshy leaves clustered at branch tips and small, white, fan-shaped flowers that appear split in half, giving rise to the naupaka legend told throughout the Pacific and Caribbean. White, spongy, buoyant fruit follow the flowers and are dispersed by ocean currents, part of the plant's natural strategy for colonizing new shorelines. This native Atlantic and Caribbean species is an important dune stabilizer and is increasingly planted specifically to displace the ecologically invasive Pacific naupaka (Scaevola taccada), so confirm the scientific name at purchase before planting. It tolerates salt spray, sandy soil, and drought once established but is frost-tender and limited to essentially frost-free coastal sites.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant nursery starts in spring into loose, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun on dunes or sandy coastal ground; beach croton is a foundational Gulf and South Atlantic dune-building shrub, not the tropical ornamental Codiaeum croton sold as a houseplant.

directions: Plant in loose, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun on dunes or other sandy coastal ground; beach croton is a rounded, silvery-gray, aromatic native shrub covered in fine star-shaped scales that reflect intense sun and salt spray, distinct from the colorful tropical houseplant croton (Codiaeum) sold under the same common name. Small, inconspicuous cream-colored flowers appear nearly year-round in mild climates, and the plant serves as a critical host for several coastal butterfly species while its extensive root system helps trap wind-blown sand and build and stabilize foredunes. It is exceptionally salt and drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation once established in appropriate sandy, well-drained soil, making it valuable for beachfront restoration and low-maintenance coastal landscaping. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, or regular watering, all of which shorten its life in this sand-adapted pioneer species.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant nursery starts in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun in essentially frost-free coastal sites; bay cedar is a pantropical strand shrub found along the immediate coastline from South Florida through the Caribbean and Gulf.

directions: Plant in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun along the immediate coastline; bay cedar is a dense, rounded, salt-tolerant strand shrub with soft, narrow, yellow-green leaves clustered toward branch tips and small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers produced nearly continuously in warm weather. It forms a natural windbreak hedge along tropical and subtropical shorelines, tolerating direct salt spray, poor sandy soil, and drought that would quickly kill most ornamental shrubs, and it requires essentially no irrigation once established. Small, dry, corky fruit follow the flowers and float on ocean currents to colonize new shoreline, the same strategy used by many other strand-zone pioneer species. Because it is strictly frost-tender, grow it only in true frost-free coastal gardens or as a large container specimen brought under cover elsewhere; light trimming after major growth flushes keeps the naturally rounded form dense.
